title: The restructure nobody explained
text:
The email arrived on a Friday afternoon: three departments merged into two, effective the first of next month. It was 90 words long and used the word "synergies" twice.

By Monday, four people had updated their profiles on job sites.

The problem was not the restructure. Most staff agreed the old org chart made little sense, and two teams had been doing overlapping work for years. The problem was that nobody explained what it meant for individual jobs.

The new head of operations noticed the silence and did something unusual. She held a town hall with no slides and answered questions for 50 minutes, including the uncomfortable ones. Would headcount fall? Yes, by six roles, all through natural departures, none forced. Would anyone's line manager change? Yes, eleven people, and each would hear directly before the end of the week.

She was not able to promise everything would be fine. She was able to say exactly what she knew and exactly what she didn't.

Two of the four job seekers stayed. When asked why, one said the answer was simple: for the first time in a year, somebody told him the truth in a room where he could ask a follow-up question.

questions.q: What was the real problem with the restructure?
options: Nobody explained what it meant for individual jobs
The new structure made no sense

questions.q: How would the headcount reduction happen?
What was unusual about the town hall?
options: No slides and honest answers to hard questions

questions.q: Why did one employee decide to stay?
options: He was told the truth and could ask questions

title: Walking away
text:
The negotiation had been running for five weeks. A large retail chain wanted English training for 120 staff across nine locations, and the contract was worth more than everything the school had earned that year.

At the fourth meeting, procurement made a counteroffer: the same programme at 38% below the quoted price, with payment 90 days after delivery.

The director asked for a day to think. That evening she wrote down two numbers: the price at which the project made sense, and the price below which it would quietly damage the business by taking teachers away from profitable work.

The counteroffer sat well below the second number.

The next morning she said no, politely and without a long explanation. She offered a smaller version instead: three locations, same rate, with an option to extend. Procurement said they would come back to her. They didn't, for six weeks.

Then they did. The smaller version was approved, and by the following spring it had grown to seven locations at the original rate.

Her leverage was never a clever argument. It was knowing her walk away price before she entered the room.

questions.q: What did procurement propose at the fourth meeting?
options: A longer contract at the same rate

questions.q: What two numbers did the director write down?
options: The price that worked and the price that would harm the business
The client's budget and her own
Last year's revenue and this year's target

questions.q: What did she offer instead of accepting?
options: A smaller version at the same rate
The same programme at a lower rate

questions.q: According to the text, where did her leverage come from?
options: Knowing her walk away price in advance
A clever argument in the meeting
